description:
We are a team of students interested in space exploration, engineering, physics, technology. Last year, we participated in a space hackathon, where we developed Infinity Nomads, a project focused on designing a sustainable space station near Europa, one of Jupiter's moons. We researched energy production, radiation protection, life support systems, and the challenges of living in space.

Our team has experience in scientific research, robotics, mathematics, data analysis, engineering design.
summary:
Astralis: Mars Orbit is a browser game for the "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge. Students aged 7 to 12 run an orbital outpost near Mars with a crew of six astronauts. Power, oxygen, water, food, research and radiation protection all share one electrical grid and one crew, so every choice has a cost. Powering the greenhouses drains the battery that has to carry the station through the 54-minute shadow of Mars. Hiding from a solar storm protects the crew but stops research and repairs.
Each mission replays a real stretch of solar activity from NASA's DONKI database, and a Live mission covers the Sun's last 30 days. Storm warnings arrive with the real Earth–Mars light delay, and only while the Earth link is switched on. Orbits, power and life support are calculated from NASA reference values. A simple view, previews that show what each switch gains and loses, and a debrief that traces the cause of a failure let children learn by causing problems and fixing them.
It matters because the real dilemmas of keeping astronauts alive become choices a child can feel, which builds systems thinking for future explorers.
details:
Astralis: Mars Orbit is a browser-based educational game for children aged 7 to 12 (and anyone curious about space). The player runs a rotating orbital station near Mars with a crew of six astronauts and has to keep power, oxygen, water, food, research and radiation protection in balance. Nothing is built: the station already exists, and the whole game is about running it and living with the consequences of each decision.

How it works. Every mission replays a real stretch of solar activity from NASA's DONKI database (September 2017, March 2012, Halloween 2021, May 2024), and a live mission plays the last 30 days of the real Sun. Storm warnings arrive with the real Earth–Mars light delay of 3 to 22 minutes, and only while the Earth link is switched on. Every 7.7-hour orbit the station passes through the shadow of Mars and its solar panels stop working for up to 54 minutes, so the battery and the player's planning matter. When a storm is coming, the player chooses: hide now, hide just in time, or keep working. Each choice has a cost in radiation dose, lost research and lost repairs. Before any switch, the game shows what the player will gain and lose. At the end, a mission report (or a debrief after a collapse) shows the turning point of the run.

Benefits and intended impact. Instead of memorising facts, students learn by causing problems and fixing them: the systems of a station depend on each other, improving one thing usually makes another worse, a reserve is needed even when things look fine, and protection has a price. A simple view with three large gauges and plain-language hints makes it playable for young children, with a teacher or parent nearby. It runs in any modern browser, on computers and phones, with no installation, so it works in a classroom.

Tools. The simulation engine is written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly, running in a separate browser thread. The 3D scene and interface use JavaScript and Three.js (WebGPU, with WebGL2 as a fallback). Mars is drawn at real scale using Viking colour and MOLA elevation data, with stars from the HYG catalogue. The station model is generated with Python, and the site is hosted on Vercel with a small server function that caches NASA data.

Creativity. Real space weather becomes gameplay: every storm in the game actually happened. Six astronauts are simulated individually, each with their own needs, mood and radiation dose, and the station's numbers are derived from NASA reference values (BVAD life-support data, ISS water recovery, Fission Surface Power, Curiosity RAD measurements).

Factors we considered. Scientific honesty: every value has a source, and the values we chose ourselves are marked as estimates. Age-appropriate design: no crew deaths, plain words, tap-to-read explanations. Reproducibility: the same seed gives the same result, and an automated test plays every mission with eight strategies. We also state the open limits openly: the radiation model is simplified, effects on health are not modelled, and the game has not yet been tested with children.
